title: USPS “incomplete address” text
setup: You're not expecting anything, but this text shows up.

content.body: USPS: Your package is on hold due to an incomplete address. Update your details within 12 hours or it will be returned to sender.

options.label: Tap the link and update your address
options.feedback: The fake site asked for a small “redelivery fee” and stole your card number.

options.label: Delete it and report it as junk
options.feedback: USPS doesn't text you unless you signed up for tracking on a specific package. This was a smishing text.

options.label: Reply asking which package it is
options.feedback: No money lost, but replying tells scammers a real person has this number.

redFlags: You never asked USPS for text updates
Unknown number and a strange .top web address
safestAction: Don't tap. Track real packages at usps.com with a tracking number you already have. Forward the text to 7726.

title: Unpaid toll text
setup: You did drive on a toll road last week. Then this arrives.

content.body: Toll Services: You have an outstanding toll balance of $6.99. To avoid a late fee of $50.00 and possible license action, pay today:

options.label: Pay the $6.99 — it's small and you did drive a toll road
options.feedback: The $6.99 was bait. The site captured your card and ran up charges.

options.label: Ignore the link. Check your account in your toll agency's official app
options.feedback: If you owed anything, it would show in your real account. Going direct beats any link.

options.label: Tap the link just to see if the site looks real
options.feedback: You didn't pay, but scam sites can look perfect. Tapping gains nothing and risks a lot.

redFlags: Small, believable amount plus a big late-fee threat
Sent from a regular phone number
Web address isn't your state's real toll site
safestAction: Don't click. Log in to your toll account through the official app or a website you type in yourself.

followUps.setup: An hour after you paid the $6.99, your phone rings.

messages.text: We're seeing unusual charges on the card you used a moment ago. To block them, I'm sending a six-digit code.
Read it back to me and I'll stop the transactions.

options.label: Read them the code so they can block it
options.feedback: The code authorized them, not the block. Paying a scam site often books you a follow-up call — they know exactly which card you used.

options.label: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card
options.feedback: Right. Your real bank cancelled the card. Nobody legitimate ever needs a code read back to them.

followUps.setup: The page opens. It looks exactly like your toll agency's site, down to the logo.

content.subject: Outstanding balance: $6.99
content.body: Enter your card details to clear your balance and avoid a $50.00 late fee. Your plate number has been pre-filled.

options.label: Pay — it has your plate number, so it must be real
options.feedback: Plate numbers are guessable or bought in bulk. A detail that looks personal is a tactic, not proof.

options.label: Close it and check your account in the official toll app
options.feedback: Exactly. A convincing page proves nothing — the address was still wrong, and your real account showed no balance.

title: USPS delivery update you asked for
setup: Yesterday you texted your tracking number to USPS (28777) to get updates. Today:

messages.text: USPS: Your item 9400100000000000000000 was delivered in or at the mailbox at 2:14 pm in your city. Reply STOP to cancel.

options.label: Go check your mailbox
options.feedback: You started this conversation with the real USPS short code, and it asks nothing of you. Nothing to fear.

options.label: Block the number — USPS never texts
options.feedback: USPS does text when you sign up for tracking. Blocking just means no more updates you asked for.

options.label: Forward it to 7726 as spam
options.feedback: This one's real. Reporting legitimate texts doesn't hurt you, but it wasn't needed.

redFlags: It comes from USPS's official short code 28777
No link, no fee, no request for info
safestAction: Real updates you signed up for are fine. The tell is whether you started it and whether it asks for money or info.

title: Shipping confirmation for your order
setup: Two days ago you ordered running shoes from ShopMart's app. This email arrives.

content.subject: Your order has shipped
content.body: Good news! Your order #58-2231-907 (Trail Runner 3, Size 9) is on its way. Estimated delivery: Thursday. You can track it anytime in the ShopMart app under Orders.
content.footer: We'll never ask for your password or payment details by email.

options.label: Open the ShopMart app and check your orders
options.feedback: It matches an order you really placed, and checking in the app confirms it without clicking anything.

options.label: Report it as phishing and delete it
options.feedback: This one was real. No harm done, but a quick look in the app would have told you.

options.label: Reply with your card number to confirm the order
options.feedback: Even with a real company, email is not a safe place for card numbers. It was exposed and misused.

redFlags: Matches an order you actually placed
Correct item details and no request for payment
Tells you to use the app you already have
safestAction: When a message matches something you did, confirm in the company's app or site — still the safest habit.

title: Mystery package with a QR code
setup: A package you didn't order shows up with cheap earbuds inside, plus this card.

content.subject: Surprise! Someone sent you a gift
content.body: Scan to find out who sent it and claim your bonus reward.
content.sender: A printed card tucked inside the box

options.label: Scan it — you're curious who sent it
options.feedback: The page asked you to “log in to claim” and captured your account password and card details.

options.label: Don't scan it. Keep the item and check your accounts for anything odd
options.feedback: You can legally keep unordered items. Skipping the QR code and watching your accounts is exactly right.

options.label: Scan it but don't enter anything
options.feedback: You got lucky. Malicious pages can still try to download harmful files or trick you a few taps later.

redFlags: Package you never ordered (a brushing scam)
QR code promising a reward or a “reveal”
Link goes to a random .shop site
safestAction: Don't scan unexpected QR codes. You don't have to pay for or return unordered items. Check your accounts and credit report.

title: Customs fee to release a package
setup: You ordered something from overseas last month. Today:

content.subject: Shipment held: customs duty unpaid ($3.25)
content.body: Your international shipment is being held at the customs facility. An import duty of $3.25 must be paid before delivery. Unclaimed shipments are destroyed after 3 days.

options.label: Pay the $3.25 so the package isn't destroyed
options.feedback: The tiny fee got your card number. The real charges came later.

options.label: Look up your order in the store's app and use the tracking it gives you
options.feedback: The store's real tracking comes from the real carrier. If there were a fee, you'd see it there.

options.label: Forward it to a friend and ask what they think
options.feedback: No harm yet, but it doesn't get you an answer. Checking the real order does.

redFlags: Tiny fee meant to seem harmless
Countdown threat to destroy your package
Sender domain doesn't match any carrier you used
safestAction: Track packages only with the tracking number from the store where you ordered, on the carrier's real website.
